01: This is a completely empty system — no suppliers, no tenders, no staff except one administrator. Everything you are about to see gets created in front of you.
02: Every deployment tells you exactly which build it is, and this page is reachable without signing in — which matters when the thing you are reporting is that you cannot sign in.
03: The product is Arabic-first. It asks once, in both languages, because a language chooser written only in the language you cannot read is no use to anybody.
04: The administrator is the only account that exists on a fresh install, and it is the only role for which two-factor authentication is compulsory.
05: Nothing procurement-shaped can exist before a buying body does — an organization is the boundary every tender query is scoped by.
06: One directorate, created in about ten seconds. Staff invited into it inherit its scope automatically.
07: There is no self-service route to a ministry account. Registration only ever creates a supplier, so every member of staff here is invited by name.
08: Six invitations, one email each with a single-use link. Until someone accepts and sets a password, that invitation is not a live account.
09: Now we switch sides. This is the supplier's first contact with the ministry — and the only self-service sign-up in the product.
10: The company name is asked in both Arabic and English because it will appear on a tender record that has to read correctly in either.
11: The account exists but cannot sign in yet. Nothing is trusted until the address is proven.
12: Verified. The supplier is now in Draft — registered, but not yet allowed anywhere near a tender.
13: An honest empty state. It tells the supplier what to do next rather than showing them a dashboard of zeroes.
14: This checklist is the gate. Every item on it is a condition the server enforces at submission — the screen and the rule cannot drift apart.
15: The legal identity — this is the block a reviewer will check against the registration certificate.
16: The default currency matters later: a bid is priced in it, and the award is issued in it.
17: A named representative. This is the person a buyer addresses a clarification to.
18: An approved supplier with no registered address is not something a ministry should be able to create, so the address is a completeness condition.
19: Where an award would actually be paid. The account number is masked everywhere it is shown again — including on the reviewer's screen.
20: Categories are chosen from the ministry's own list, not typed. That is what makes invitations targetable later.
21: One item off the checklist. Notice the completeness figure moving as we go.
22: The file went to object storage and was virus-scanned before it was accepted. If the scanner is down, the upload is refused — I will come back to that at the end.
23: Accepting the terms is recorded against a named version and a timestamp. The tick on screen is not the acceptance; the record is.
24: Only now does Submit appear. The server enforces the same condition, so this is not the button being polite.
25: Submitted. The profile is read-only from here — the supplier cannot edit what is being judged while it is being judged.
26: Now the reviewer. Notice how little this persona can reach: two links, both about reviewing suppliers.
27: This dashboard existed for two batches and nothing in the application linked to it. Nobody could reach it without typing the address.
28: One application waiting — the one we created five minutes ago. The queue is scoped: a reviewer sees applications, never tenders.
29: The entire submitted profile in one place, with every document downloadable. This is the screen the compliance decision is actually made on.
30: Claimed. The decision controls appear only after the reviewer takes the case, which is what stops two reviewers working on the same application.
31: Approved, with a written reason recorded against the decision. An approval nobody can account for later is not much of an approval.
32: Ticking a category said what this company does in principle. An offering is the concrete thing it sells — and it is what actually makes them findable.
33: The company is now visible to buyers. A tender carrying this category will suggest this supplier to the officer writing it.
34: How bids will be scored is decided before any bid exists, and by the manager — not by the officer who writes the tender.
35: A draft template scores nothing. The weights have to total one hundred before it can be used.
36: Two criteria, across two of the four dimensions the product offers: technical, commercial, compliance and delivery.
37: Activated, and frozen from here. A tender that binds this template keeps this exact set of criteria even if somebody edits the template tomorrow.
38: The procurement officer. This is the persona that does the day-to-day work of running a tender.
39: Another screen that was built, permissioned and unreachable until batch twelve. It is the officer's home page.
40: No tenders exist. Everything you have seen so far was created through these screens, in this order.
41: The reference code is allocated by the server, not typed. It is the code that appears in every email and every export from here on.
42: In Draft, everything is editable and nobody outside this office can see any of it.
43: One line, priced per pupil per day, with a quantity for the school year. Bids are priced against these lines.
44: A requirement is answered in prose and scored by an evaluator — that is what makes it different from a line item.
45: The specification suppliers will bid against. Scanned on upload like every other file, and it becomes part of the published tender.
46: The tender now carries the criteria it will be judged by. Bidders can see them, which is deliberate — nobody is scored against a rule they were not told.
47: Invited by name from the approved list. A tender cannot be sent to a company that has not been through onboarding.
48: Submitted for review, and the officer can no longer edit it. Authorship and approval are separate jobs.
49: The manager sees the same tender with different controls: approve, or send back for edits.
50: Approved — but not yet visible to any supplier. Approval and publication are two steps on purpose.
51: Published. The submission window opens on its own when the start time passes; a scheduled job moves it, not a person.
52: There it is — the job ran and the window is open. That is the system's clock, not ours.
53: Back to the supplier. They see this tender because they were invited to it; an uninvited company sees nothing at all.
54: The same tender from the other side: the lines to price, the requirements to answer, the deadline, and the specification to download.
55: A question, recorded against the tender. The supplier cannot see other bidders' questions until an answer is published.
56: The buyer sees the question. Who asked it is deliberately not shown — and here is why that matters.
57: One answer, published to every invited supplier at once, with the asker anonymised. Nobody gets an advantage by asking, and nobody is discouraged from asking.
58: And here is that answer arriving on the supplier's side, attributed to the buyer rather than to whoever asked.
59: A draft bid, private to this supplier. Notice the two envelopes as separate sections — technical and commercial.
60: A unit price against the buyer's line. The total is derived from the quantity on the tender, not typed by the bidder.
61: The technical half of the bid. This is what an evaluator scores, and it stays sealed from the price until the technical stage is passed.
62: Payment terms and a supporting certificate. Everything a bid consists of is now on the record — and still editable.
63: Submitted, and read-only from here. This is the moment the bid becomes evidence rather than a draft.
64: Closed early by the officer rather than waiting out the clock. Bids are fixed now; nothing further can arrive.
65: The evaluation exists, carrying the criteria frozen when the template was bound. No scores yet.
66: Assigned by name, and only from staff who actually hold the scoring permission in this buying body.
67: The evaluator's world is deliberately small: their assignments, and almost nothing else.
68: The conflict declaration comes before a single bid is visible, and it names the bidders — because that is the information somebody needs in order to declare a conflict.
69: Bidders anonymous, price locked. The evaluator is judging the answer, not the company and not the number.
70: The technical score is in, and the price is still sealed.
71: The financial criterion unlocked only because this bid passed technically. That order is enforced, not conventional.
72: Submitted. Scores cannot be revised after this without a manager reopening the evaluation, and that reopening is recorded.
73: Consolidation is the moment the two envelopes are put together — technical scores and prices weighted into one ranking.
74: Bids side by side, identified by proposal reference rather than company name. This is the screen a procurement decision is defended from.
75: The manager closes the shortlist and fixes the ranking — not the officer who ran the evaluation.
76: The award screen before any decision has been taken. Nobody is recommended yet.
77: A recommendation, with a written justification, naming the bid. It decides nothing on its own.
78: Handed on. The recommender has now done everything they are allowed to do.
79: This refusal is the product working, not a fault. Segregation of duties: the person who recommends may not approve.
80: A second manager, who did not write the recommendation, sees the recommendation, the justification and the bid it names.
81: Approved by somebody other than the recommender. The tender has a winner.
82: Issued. This is the point at which the outcome leaves the building — the winner is notified and the integration message is queued.
83: The supplier sees the result of the bid they submitted. Their own price was visible to them throughout; the buyer's view of it was not.
84: The award queued an integration message, and this screen is honest about what happens to it: there is no real ERP connected yet, and it says so rather than showing a green tick.
85: The rest of the walk is each persona's own screens. This is the administrator's overview: counts, health, integrations.
86: The code lists everything else is built from — categories, document types, currencies, units, regions.
87: Any string in the product can be reworded here without a release, because the people who own the wording are not the people who deploy.
88: The transactional emails, with their required tokens shown. A save that drops the verification link is refused.
89: Every state change, with an actor and a correlation id, append-only. This is the record that makes an approval defensible a year later.
90: The buying bodies — the boundary every tender query is scoped by.
91: The Ministry's view: cross-organization totals and no commercial figures at all. That is a decision, and I will explain it at the end.
92: Back to the supplier, now with real activity: completeness, invitations, proposals, and documents needing attention.
93: The company record as its own staff see it, each section linking to the editor rather than duplicating it.
94: Every document with its state and expiry, and a filter for the ones needing attention. Expiry is the thing that quietly disqualifies a supplier.
95: The supplier invites its own colleagues. A supplier user can prepare a bid; only a supplier admin can submit one.
96: Account, language, password and active sessions — and that is the whole system, from an empty database to an issued award.
